title: Divide and Conquer and the Master Theorem

questions.question: Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges in linear time. Which recurrence describes its running time?
questions.explanation: Two subproblems (a = 2) of half the size (b = 2) plus a linear merge (f(n) = n). T(n/2) + 1 is binary search, T(n/2) + n would be a single half with a linear combine, and 2 T(n-1) + 1 is the exponential subset enumeration.

questions.question: For T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n), what does the quantity n^(log_b a) represent in the recursion tree?
options: The work done at the root level of the tree
The number of leaves, and therefore the total work the leaves do
The depth of the tree in levels
The total work summed over all levels of the tree
questions.explanation: There are a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a) leaves, each doing constant work; the master theorem compares f(n), the root's work, against this leaf work to decide which end of the tree dominates. The depth is log_b n and the total is what the theorem computes.

questions.question: Karatsuba replaces four half-size multiplications with three, keeping the O(n) additions. What happens to the running time?
options: It drops from O(n^2) to O(n log n) because the additions now dominate
It drops from Θ(n^2) to Θ(n^1.585) because the leaf count falls from n^2 to n^(log2 3)
It stays Θ(n^2) because the combine step is unchanged and the combine step sets the bound
It drops by a constant factor of 3/4 since one quarter of the multiplications is saved
questions.explanation: Both recurrences are case 1 (f = n is polynomially smaller than the critical exponent), so the leaves dominate and the answer is n^(log2 a): n^2 for a = 4, n^1.585 for a = 3. The number of subproblems sets the exponent; the combine cost only matters when it is as large as the leaf work.

questions.question: T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + n log n. Which statement is correct?
options: Case 3 applies because n log n is strictly larger than n for all large n, so the root dominates and T(n) = Θ(n log n)
Case 2 applies because n log n is asymptotically the same as n once constants are ignored, so T(n) = Θ(n log n)
No case applies because n log n exceeds n by less than any polynomial factor; the recursion tree gives Θ(n log^2 n)
Case 1 applies because log n grows more slowly than any polynomial, so the leaves dominate and T(n) = Θ(n)
questions.explanation: The three cases need f(n) to differ from n^c by a factor of n^e for some e > 0; log n is not such a factor, so the recurrence falls in the gap. Summing the tree level by level gives n(log n + (log n - 1) + ... + 1) = Θ(n log^2 n), which the extended form of case 2 also states.

questions.question: A team parallelises a linear two-pointer reconciliation by recursively splitting both lists at a matching timestamp (a linear scan) and reconciling halves on separate cores. Why is it slower?
options: Because thread creation in the JVM costs more than the reconciliation work saved by splitting
Because the recurrence is 2 T(n/2) + n, which is Θ(n log n); the log n factor exceeds the gain from 32 cores
Because recursive algorithms cannot be parallelised without a shared lock on the output
Because the lists must be re-sorted at every level, adding an n log n sort per split
questions.explanation: The split scan is a linear combine cost at every level, so the design is merge sort's recurrence and does about 28x more work than the single pass for n of a few hundred million; dividing by 32 cores does not recover it. Partitioning once into 32 ranges and running the linear merge on each is Θ(n / 32).

questions.question: Strassen's algorithm has a better exponent than the triple loop, yet a team found it slower on their matrices. What is the most likely reason?
options: Strassen only applies to matrices whose dimension is a power of two, so padding doubled their work
The triple loop is Θ(n^2) on dense matrices, which Strassen cannot beat
Strassen's seven products and eighteen additions carry a large constant and poor cache behaviour, and their n was below the crossover
Strassen requires exact rational arithmetic, which is far slower than floating point
questions.explanation: A better exponent wins only above the crossover size where the constant is amortised; for Strassen that is hundreds of rows depending on hardware, and production BLAS uses it only above a tuned threshold. Padding to a power of two is a minor cost, the triple loop is Θ(n^3), and Strassen works in any arithmetic.
